responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark faces a structural dependency on Apple and Google for digital identity access, creating supplier concentration and continuity-of-service risks that conflict with its 2026–2029 digital sovereignty agenda. The project navigates four core tensions: (1) technical feasibility versus regulatory conservatism in the MitID ecosystem, (2) demonstrator credibility versus scope creep into production features, (3) institutional influence without direct control over AltID procurement, and (4) coalition-building across divergent stakeholders (civil society, government, EU bodies) with competing timelines and incentives. The selected levers address these tensions by sequencing credible evidence production before procurement intervention, designing demonstrators to challenge incumbent assumptions rather than replace them, and structuring phase gates to preserve optionality if Danish institutional traction weakens.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Standards Choice
levers.consequences: Selecting between a single integrated platform-neutral demonstrator versus separate mobile and fallback demonstrators determines both technical credibility and resource allocation across phases two and three. A unified demonstrator runs the risk of feature creep and misses the opportunity to isolate fallback mechanisms from mobile OS constraints; separate demonstrators create more friction points but allow stronger evidence that platform-neutral access does not require abandoning mobile security entirely. This choice also signals to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen whether the project is proposing a shadow MitID replacement or a true architectural alternative.
options: Develop a single comprehensive demonstrator using FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS that mimics live MitID workflows, integrating both primary authentication and a built-in fallback path to establish that a unified stack can operate independently of Apple and Google.

Build two decoupled demonstrators: one mobile-focused on GrapheneOS using OpenID Connect and FIDO2 for day-to-day authentication, and a separate browser-based or hardware-token fallback that operates entirely outside the mobile ecosystem, each proving a distinct non-incumbent pathway.

Construct a minimal reference implementation demonstrator that authenticates against a simulated Danish identity provider using open standards, deliberately avoiding feature parity with MitID in order to focus evaluation strictly on platform neutrality and fallback feasibility without inviting scope expansion.
levers.review_lever: Separate demonstrators prove architectural independence but diffuse impact if neither reaches the maturity needed to influence AltID procurement timelines; a single demonstrator risks feature creep and losing focus on the core fallback message. The options do not address how to communicate demonstrator limitations to stakeholders who will expect production-readiness parallels.

levers.name: Coalition Structure and Civil-Society Lead
levers.consequences: Positioning civil-society organizations or academic researchers as public faces of the platform-neutrality push rather than government bodies removes the appearance of state-directed vendor selection and increases credibility with EU counterparts and regulatory bodies concerned about democratic legitimacy. However, this also transfers agenda-setting power away from the project team and may slow institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen if civil-society co-leads pursue privacy or ideological framings that diverge from the project's resilience-and-procurement emphasis. A weak civil-society coalition risks the appearance of a vendor-driven or academic paper exercise rather than a genuine public-interest intervention.
options: Anchor the coalition with a respected Danish civil-society organization such as a privacy advocate or digital rights group as co-lead, with the project team in a technical-support role, and explicitly structure monthly public reporting to maintain independence optics and EU visibility.

Distribute leadership across three nodes: an academic security researcher heading technical work, a civil-society privacy advocate leading public advocacy, and a procurement or resilience specialist engaging Digitaliseringsstyrelsen directly, to create multiple credibility streams without a single point of failure.

Maintain the project team as the primary institutional actor and recruit civil-society and academic advisors into a formal steering committee with public membership and quarterly meetings, reserving procurement engagement for the project lead to ensure message coherence and continuity.
levers.review_lever: Civil-society co-leadership increases legitimacy but diffuses control and may introduce competing narratives that undermine procurement messaging; team-led models with advisory structures risk appearing state-captured if Digitaliseringsstyrelsen is perceived as controlling the agenda. None of the options address how to manage tensions if civil-society partners want stronger public advocacy than procurement timing allows.

levers.name: Phase-Two Demonstrator Platform and Operating-System Choice
levers.consequences: Selecting GrapheneOS, Lineage OS, or another privacy-respecting Android fork versus attempting iOS compatibility or a web-only approach determines the demonstrator's technical defensibility and political acceptability. GrapheneOS carries stronger privacy credentials and independence from Google Play but is less familiar to Danish public-sector evaluators and carries a perception of niche adoption; a broader Android fork reduces that friction but weakens the platform-independence claim if it still relies on Google APIs. A web-only approach avoids OS lock-in entirely but loses credibility in a mobile-first authentication environment where citizens expect app-based security. The choice shapes both technical scope and stakeholder perception of whether fallback pathways are realistic or fringe.
options: Implement the primary demonstrator on GrapheneOS using only GrapheneOS-native security APIs and open-standards authentication, accepting reduced familiarity among Danish stakeholders in exchange for the strongest technical case that mobile authentication does not require Google or Apple dependencies.

Deploy the demonstrator on LineageOS or another widely available Android fork that supports F-Droid app distribution, reducing barriers to stakeholder comprehension while maintaining the core claim that Android-based authentication can operate without Play Store or Google Play Services dependency.

Build a browser-based progressive web app (PWA) or hybrid web/native demonstrator that minimizes OS-level dependencies altogether and works across both iOS and Android through standard web authentication APIs, prioritizing cross-platform accessibility over the statement that mobile OS independence is required.
levers.review_lever: GrapheneOS maximizes platform-independence credibility but introduces adoption and perception barriers among non-specialist evaluators; web-based approaches broaden accessibility but weaken the argument that mobile-OS duopoly dependence is the core problem. The options do not resolve whether demonstrator credibility is measured by technical purity or by stakeholder adoption signals that could compromise the independence message.

levers.name: Engagement Timing and Institutional Lead Target
levers.consequences: Approaching Digitaliseringsstyrelsen early in phase one versus waiting until demonstrators are complete and phase-two evidence is solid determines whether the project influences AltID procurement direction upstream or arrives as a critique of decisions already locked in. Early engagement risks being seen as premature or proposal-driven without technical backing; late engagement maximizes demonstrator credibility but may miss critical procurement-decision windows. The choice also depends on whether MitID's operator or other incumbent bodies perceive the project as collaborative exploration or as a threat to existing contracts and operator revenue. Misaligned timing can result in either dismissal due to lack of evidence or procedural opposition once institutional commitments harden.
options: Initiate formal engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the AltID program office during phase one using the feasibility report and institutional risk framing as the opening conversation, positioning the project as a resilience partner and inviting early procurement language discussions before AltID design is finalized.

Defer direct institutional engagement until the end of phase two when demonstrators and the full feasibility report are complete, then approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen with concrete technical evidence and a formal procurement-language proposal, trading early influence for higher credibility and reduced risk of early dismissal.

Pursue a two-stage engagement: informal early discussions with sympathetic Digitaliseringsstyrelsen staff during phase one to understand procurement timelines and decision gates, followed by formal proposals and demonstrator evidence at critical phase gates, allowing the project to adapt tactics based on institutional receptiveness without premature commitment.
levers.review_lever: Early engagement can shape procurement language but risks premature dismissal if evidence is incomplete; late engagement ensures credibility but may miss decision windows. The options do not address how to recover or pivot if institutional receptiveness shifts due to political or budgetary changes unrelated to the project's merit.

levers.name: EU Standards and Interoperability Positioning
levers.consequences: Framing the platform-neutrality requirement as a European Digital Identity Wallet interoperability and resilience mandate versus a Danish-specific sovereignty concern determines whether the project seeks EU-level standards alignment or focuses narrowly on Danish procurement. EU-level positioning increases the project's legitimacy and difficulty for vendors to dismiss as parochial; it also aligns with Denmark's 2026–2029 strategy and may create pressure on AltID through EU frameworks rather than direct Danish procurement influence. However, EU-level work is slower, requires coordination with multiple member states, and may be pre-empted by incumbent vendor relationships and EU-level standardization bodies already dominated by commercial platforms. A Danish-focused narrative is faster and more controllable but risks being dismissed as a small-country concern that does not generalize.
options: Center phase three on formal submissions and technical comments to the European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and relevant eIDAS2 standards bodies, positioning platform neutrality and fallback access as EU-wide resilience requirements that will set a floor for all member-state implementations including Denmark.

Pursue parallel Danish and EU engagement: maintain AltID-focused procurement language at the Danish level while contributing to EU standards discussions as supporting evidence, avoiding over-commitment to EU-level processes that may not align with Danish phase timelines.

Prioritize Danish AltID and procurement intervention as the primary lever and treat EU engagement as a secondary dissemination channel for demonstrators and feasibility findings, accepting that EU influence is longer-term and lower-probability than direct Danish institutional impact.
levers.review_lever: EU-level positioning increases legitimacy and spreads advocacy pressure but operates on slower timelines that may not align with AltID procurement gates; Danish-focused approaches are faster but risk being dismissed as parochial. The options do not address how to manage misalignment if EU standards work and Danish procurement proceed on incompatible timelines.

levers.name: External Security Review and Third-Party Credibility
levers.consequences: Commissioning an independent security assessment of demonstrators and feasibility findings from a credible external firm or academic institution versus relying on internal review and peer publication increases stakeholder confidence and reduces the risk that Digitaliseringsstyrelsen dismisses the work as self-interested or technically naive. An external review adds cost and timeline delay, and the choice of reviewer shapes perception—a firm with vendor relationships may be perceived as conflicted, while a pure academic body may lack procurement credibility. The review's findings also create a public record that can be cited for or against the project if institutional politics shift, making the timing and scope of external review a strategic choice with political consequences.
options: Commission a formal independent security audit and feasibility assessment from a respected third-party firm such as a Danish or Nordic security consultancy or academic security lab, with public release of findings and explicit scope covering demonstrators, fallback-mechanism soundness, and platform-independence claims.

Pair internal technical review with peer publication in recognized academic conferences and journals, allowing the academic community to vet the work's technical merit while maintaining faster timelines and lower cost than commercial audit, accepting reduced procurement-level credibility.

Engage a panel of external advisors from academia, cybersecurity, and procurement domains for ongoing review throughout phases two and three, publishing findings incrementally rather than a single comprehensive audit, spreading credibility-building across multiple sources and timelines.
levers.review_lever: Commercial external audit maximizes procurement credibility but adds cost and timeline risk; academic peer review is faster and lower-cost but may lack direct procurement influence. The options do not address how to respond if external findings are negative or identify technical gaps that require scope expansion or delay.

levers.name: Fallback Mechanism Design Philosophy and Fallback Trigger Conditions
levers.consequences: Designing the fallback authentication path as a transparent citizen-selectable option available at initial login versus a system-initiated emergency failover triggered only when primary authentication fails determines both user-experience friction and institutional resistance to the fallback requirement. Transparent choice creates a UX and policy narrative that supports genuine optionality and digital autonomy; it also allows supporters to frame fallback as empowerment rather than a compromise path. However, incumbent operators and platform vendors may resist a design that positions platform-dependent authentication as optional rather than default, fearing reduced platform engagement. A system-triggered failover design is less disruptive to incumbent expectations but weakens the political case for platform neutrality by hiding the fallback mechanism and limiting its visibility as a credible alternative. The fallback-trigger conditions also determine whether the fallback path is truly platform-neutral or merely a temporary workaround for edge cases.
options: Design the fallback mechanism as a citizen-facing option available at initial login, allowing users to authenticate through browser-based OpenID Connect or hardware-token methods without requiring the mobile app, with clear labeling of platform dependencies so citizens understand the security and autonomy trade-offs.

Implement the fallback as a system-initiated automatic failover triggered when the primary mobile authentication path fails or is unavailable, maintaining the platform-dependent primary path as default while ensuring fallback capacity exists, positioning resilience as an invisible contingency rather than a citizen choice.

Structure the fallback authentication path as a complete alternative flow with separate enrollment, credential issuance, and public communication, allowing citizens and institutions to treat fallback and primary paths as equally legitimate entry points, with coordinated messaging that platform neutrality is a design principle rather than an emergency measure.
levers.review_lever: Transparent citizen choice maximizes policy legitimacy but invites institutional resistance and complicates adoption messaging; automatic failover reduces friction with incumbents but weakens the political case that platform neutrality is essential. The options do not address how to manage security perception gaps if citizens or evaluators interpret fallback mechanisms as second-class authentication compared to the primary mobile path.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity infrastructure faces a critical single-point-of-failure risk: Apple and Google control not just app distribution but the integrity signals, push-notification pathways, and platform-level trust anchors that underpin MitID. The project's core tension is between technical feasibility (platform-neutral fallbacks are architecturally possible) and institutional capture (regulators, operators, and procurement bodies default to the incumbent duopoly because it appears mature and risk-free). The selected levers address how to overcome this institutional inertia: who leads the demonstrator work and how credibly, when and how to engage institutional gatekeepers before they harden requirements around Apple/Google, whether to frame the problem as security/resilience or sovereignty/procurement, how to position fallback mechanisms so they feel like insurance rather than rebellion, what external legitimacy (academic, security community, EU bodies) shifts the burden of proof onto platform dependence, and whether to pursue incremental AltID influence or pivot toward EU-level standards pressure if Danish institutional capture proves intractable. Success requires simultaneous technical credibility, policy narrative control, and strategic timing—pulling the wrong lever at the wrong moment locks in platform dependence for another generation.

levers.name: Demonstrator Authenticity and Security Pedigree
levers.consequences: The credibility of platform-neutral fallback authentication rests entirely on whether skeptical regulators and operators believe the demonstrators represent genuinely secure alternatives, not security theater or ideological proof-of-concept. A demonstrator built by academic researchers with published cryptographic credentials and external security review generates institutional weight; one built without formal adversarial review or by unknown contributors becomes ammunition for incumbent operators to dismiss as immature or unvetted. The choice determines whether AltID stakeholders and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen treat the work as a credible technical baseline or as activist posturing.
options: Commission an independent third-party security audit (e.g., by a recognized security firm or university security lab with published eIDAS/NSIS expertise) of both demonstrators before phase two completion, with findings published alongside the project outputs to establish institutional credibility and shift the burden of evidence onto platform-dependent alternatives.

Embed a security researcher with established peer-reviewed publication record on mobile authentication, FIDO2, or eIDAS as a co-lead of the demonstrator work, ensuring that cryptographic design and threat modeling are defensible in academic and regulatory contexts from project inception.

Pursue a lightweight self-assessment and fuzzing protocol covering the demonstrators' authentication logic, publish the methodology and results transparently, and invite the security research community to contribute independent validation through a public code repository and open-call bug-bounty period.
levers.review_lever: Third-party audit provides highest institutional weight but delays phase-two timeline and costs 150k–250k DKK; academia-led design builds credibility incrementally but depends on finding a suitable researcher and may not satisfy procurement-minded regulators who want formal certification pathways. All three leave open the gap of productization: demonstrators need not and should not be production-ready, but regulators will use lack of operational maturity against fallback-capable design, regardless of security pedigree.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Posture and Regulatory Window
levers.consequences: Phase two demonstrators are complete by month 16; AltID procurement and technical specifications are being finalized around months 14–18. This window is narrow and non-recoverable—if the project fails to inject platform-neutrality language or fallback-access requirements into AltID design documents or procurement criteria by month 18, the next identity refresh cycle is likely 5–10 years away. Engagement posture determines whether the project appears as a constructive technical contributor (raising AltID resilience) or an external pressure campaign (triggering defensive stonewalling from incumbent operators and procurement gatekeepers). Misjudging tone or timing converts technical work into political liability.
options: Present demonstrators and feasibility findings to AltID's technical working group and procurement team in month 15 as optional resilience enhancements and fallback pathways, framing platform-neutrality as a continuity insurance policy rather than a criticism of existing MitID, and negotiate for inclusion as a non-mandatory secondary authentication layer or contingency plan in procurement language.

Escalate the platform-dependency issue to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's digital-strategy unit and to Finanstilsynet (the financial regulator) in month 14, positioning the demonstrators as evidence supporting mandatory supplier-diversification and fallback requirements in upcoming procurement rules, and use regulatory pressure as leverage to force AltID procurement teams to justify their platform choices.

Withhold direct engagement with AltID until phase two demonstrates working fallback authentication at a technical conference or academic venue, then use external validation and media attention to create a reputational cost for AltID if it ignores platform-neutral alternatives, forcing a late-cycle procurement amendment or design reconsideration driven by public-sector reputation management.
levers.review_lever: Constructive engagement risks being ignored if procurement teams perceive no downside cost to platform dependence; regulatory escalation invites institutional backlash and may harden opposition; public-shaming via external validation depends on media traction and may backfire if perceived as grandstanding rather than substance. None addresses the core blocker: that MitID operators control AltID's technical direction and have financial incentives to perpetuate platform duopoly lock-in.

levers.name: Fallback-Mechanism Role and Certification Pathway
levers.consequences: A fallback authentication path can be positioned as either a mandatory, always-available alternative to app-based authentication (requiring formal certification and integration into MitID or AltID trust frameworks) or as an optional, contingency-only mechanism (triggered only if primary path fails, reducing certification burden but also reducing institutional weight and pre-emptive impact). The former increases relevance and guarantees that the fallback is actually deployed and maintained; the latter preserves optionality and avoids forcing MitID operators to defend why their primary path is not platform-neutral. The positioning shapes whether the project influences day-to-day authentication behavior or remains a theoretical insurance policy that operators and citizens ignore unless forced to use it.
options: Design the fallback mechanism as a mandatory secondary authentication option available to all citizens for critical transactions (e.g., tax filing, medical data access), require formal integration into MitID's or AltID's certification and trust-evaluation framework, and pursue formal approval from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen as a regulatory requirement rather than an optional feature.

Position the fallback mechanism as a declared contingency path activated only during documented platform outages or supplier policy changes that affect citizen access, reducing immediate certification friction but requiring pre-positioned legal and technical infrastructure so that fallback deployment does not become a multi-month crisis response if the contingency is triggered.

Develop the fallback as a progressive-enhancement fallback embedded in the browser-based eIDAS2 wallet reference architecture rather than as a MitID alternative, allowing it to exist in the EU standards layer and circumvent formal Danish MitID certification gates, accepting lower near-term institutional impact in exchange for longer-term EU-level influence over digital identity portability.
levers.review_lever: Mandatory integration forces a choice that incumbent operators will resist; contingency-only positioning reduces pressure but risks abandonment if the contingency never materializes; EU-layer design avoids Danish gatekeepers but delays measurable impact on AltID and leaves Danish citizens exposed for years. All three leave unresolved the question of whether citizens or regulators will actually use a fallback mechanism if it exists—convenience and habit favor the incumbent duopoly even if alternatives are available.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Advocacy Leadership
levers.consequences: A coalition spanning civil-society privacy advocates, contingency-planning authorities, academic security researchers, and sympathetic MPs creates multiple institutional entry points for platform-neutrality arguments and reduces the project's appearance as a single-organization campaign. The coalition's composition also signals credibility: an organization led by privacy advocates may be dismissed as ideological; one led by contingency-planning authorities or a public-health regulator concerned with medical data access gains operational legitimacy. Conversely, a broad coalition risks diffuse messaging, competing priorities, and paralysis-by-consensus if partners disagree on whether to prioritize resilience, privacy, sovereignty, or cost reduction.
options: Establish a formal steering group co-led by a contingency-planning or crisis-management authority (e.g., Beredskabsstyrelsen or a regional health authority) and an established privacy or civil-rights organization, ensuring that the coalition's public-facing narrative emphasizes continuity-of-service and public-sector resilience rather than ideology, and securing institutional credibility from a government agency with explicit responsibility for backup systems and supply-chain risk.

Build a looser, decentralized coalition of individual researchers, security experts, and interested MPs rather than formal partner organizations, allowing faster decision-making and preventing institutional veto power, but accepting reduced formal institutional weight and a greater burden on the project's communications team to synthesize and coordinate messaging across independent voices.

Prioritize recruitment of technical leads from major Danish banks and critical-infrastructure operators (e.g., energy or transportation authorities) that depend on digital identity authentication for internal compliance and customer access, creating a private-sector counterweight to public-sector incumbent operators and positioning fallback authentication as a business-continuity requirement rather than a regulatory or advocacy issue.
levers.review_lever: Government co-leadership provides credibility but introduces slow decision cycles and political sensitivity; decentralized coalition enables speed but risks public perception of disorganization; private-sector engagement shifts framing but may alienate civil-society partners and create suspicion of commercial motivations. None directly addresses the core institutional asymmetry: that incumbent MitID and AltID operators have formal decision authority while the coalition has only advocacy pressure.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Sovereignty Framing
levers.consequences: The project's policy narrative can emphasize either continuity-of-service and supplier-concentration risk (resonates with procurement and risk-management officials) or digital sovereignty and reduced foreign-vendor lock-in (resonates with privacy advocates and nationalist constituencies but invites dismissal as ideological). A resilience frame centers on "what if Apple or Google change terms, restrict access, or experience regional outages?" and appeals to institutional duty to protect essential services. A sovereignty frame centers on "Danish public infrastructure should not depend on foreign corporate decisions" and appeals to democratic control but risks being labeled as xenophobic or anti-American, playing into incumbent operators' dismissal of the project as a political stunt rather than a serious security proposal.
options: Lead all policy communication and proposal language with continuity-of-service, supplier-concentration, and business-continuity framing—emphasizing that fallback authentication is insurance against platform-policy changes, outages, or geopolitical disruption—and minimize or omit sovereignty language unless specifically asked, allowing resilience arguments to dominate institutional decision-making without appearing ideologically motivated.

Frame platform-dependency as a democratic accountability and public-interest issue, emphasizing that foreign corporations should not control the trust anchors for Danish citizens' access to public services and healthcare, and ground the argument in European digital autonomy principles and eIDAS intent to reduce digital dependence on large U.S. platforms, accepting that this frame will energize privacy and digital-rights communities but may alienate procurement-focused officials.

Explicitly connect both frames in project materials—present resilience and continuity as the primary institutional rationale, but also articulate digital sovereignty as a secondary strategic objective for Denmark's 2026–2029 digital strategy, treating them as complementary rather than competing, and allow different audiences to weight them differently based on institutional mandate and values.
levers.review_lever: Pure resilience framing maximizes institutional buy-in but may be perceived as euphemistic if sovereignty is the actual primary concern; sovereignty framing energizes political allies but invites institutional dismissal as activist rather than technical; dual framing attempts to satisfy both but risks appearing incoherent or opportunistic. None fully resolves the perception problem: that the project is fundamentally a challenge to incumbent operators' market position, regardless of stated rationale.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Input Versus Danish-Focused Procurement Intervention
levers.consequences: The project can allocate effort either toward influencing European Digital Identity Wallet standards, interoperability requirements, and eIDAS2 implementation rules (higher institutional reach, longer timelines, lower direct impact on Danish AltID) or toward directly engaging Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, MitID operators, and AltID procurement (faster feedback loop, higher direct impact, but limited to Danish institutional scope and dependent on political will of a small number of gatekeepers). EU-level work builds on the project's technical credibility and creates pressure on member states to adopt supplier-neutral requirements; Danish-focused work concentrates effort on the immediate decision window but accepts that a negative outcome at the Danish level cannot be overridden by EU standards later.
options: Prioritize direct engagement with Danish procurement, AltID technical teams, and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen through months 14–20, treating EU standards input as a secondary activity that leverages successful Danish precedent; accept that if Danish institutional capture occurs, the project's EU-level work becomes a consolation prize rather than the primary lever for system change.

Allocate 40–50% of phase-three effort toward formal input to the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working group, eIDAS2 national-implementation committees, and relevant EU standardization bodies (ETSI, CEN), positioning platform-neutral and fallback-capable requirements as EU-level best practices and accepting slower but broader impact that may influence Danish procurement indirectly through regulatory harmonization pressure.

Treat EU engagement and Danish procurement as parallel tracks with equal resourcing, ensuring that the project is simultaneously pressuring Danish gatekeepers and building EU-level language that makes it harder for Denmark to ignore platform-neutrality requirements, accepting overhead complexity and the risk that neither track reaches critical mass if team capacity proves insufficient to maintain momentum on both fronts.
levers.review_lever: EU-first strategy accepts weak near-term Danish impact in exchange for longer-term systemic change; Danish-first strategy risks wasting EU relationship-building effort if Danish procurement is captured; parallel tracks optimize total leverage but demand senior staff capable of navigating both Danish institutional politics and EU technical governance, a skillset gap that may not be filled within the project budget.

levers.name: Fallback Technical Architecture and Platform Dependency Trade-off
levers.consequences: A browser-based fallback authentication mechanism avoids mobile-OS dependence entirely but introduces new dependencies on web-browser vendors (Chrome, Safari) and may exclude citizens without reliable broadband or digital literacy for web authentication workflows. A hardware-token or smartcard-based fallback avoids both mobile and browser dependencies but requires physical distribution, enrollment overhead, and citizen willingness to carry an additional device—a friction cost that may limit actual adoption. A GrapheneOS-based mobile demonstrator proves that a privacy-respecting Android alternative is technically feasible but doesn't eliminate mobile-OS dependence and may face institutional resistance because GrapheneOS is perceived as niche or security-theater rather than a sustainable citizen-facing solution. The choice determines whether the fallback is truly platform-neutral or merely swaps one dependency set for another.
options: Develop the browser-based fallback mechanism as the primary technical pathway, emphasizing that web-based authentication using OpenID Connect and FIDO2 over HTTPS is the closest available path to platform-neutrality for mass-market citizen authentication, and position the GrapheneOS demonstrator as a proof-of-concept showing that mobile alternatives exist but acknowledging that browser-based workflows are more institutionally feasible.

Implement a hybrid fallback combining a lightweight hardware token (USB-C or NFC-based, compatible with existing national ID cards if technically feasible) with web-browser authentication, creating multiple independent fallback pathways so that citizens can choose based on preference and circumstance, and accepting additional complexity in demonstrator scope and certification requirements in exchange for true platform-neutrality across device types.

Prioritize the GrapheneOS-based mobile fallback as the lead technical pathway, arguing that a privacy-respecting, open-source Android variant demonstrates that app-based authentication need not depend on Google's proprietary systems and integrity APIs, and position the browser-based approach as a secondary fallback, accepting that this choice keeps fallback authentication within the mobile-OS ecosystem but substitutes open-source infrastructure for proprietary platform control.
levers.review_lever: Browser-based avoids OS lock-in but introduces new browser-vendor dependencies and digital-divide friction; hardware tokens offer true platform-independence but have high adoption friction and cost; GrapheneOS remains OS-dependent despite being open-source and may not satisfy regulatory demands for mainstream platform alternatives. All three require that regulators accept fallback mechanisms as valid alternatives rather than demanding that primary authentication remain platform-agnostic—an institutional choice none of these technical options can force.

levers.name: Funding Contingency and Project Persistence Through Institutional Delays
levers.consequences: The project's 10.5 million DKK budget is front-loaded (3.0 million phase one) with phase-three funding (3.5 million) conditional on achieving specific phase-two institutional gatekeeping criteria by month 16. If institutional progress is slower than expected—if AltID procurement is delayed, if Digitaliseringsstyrelsen response takes longer than projected, or if political support shifts—the project faces a critical decision: extend phase two demonstrator work with contingency funding, wind down and pivot toward EU-level standards work, or accept phase-three deferral and attempt to restart after political conditions improve. The funding structure determines whether the project can survive institutional inertia or whether delays automatically cascade into project failure.
options: Secure a commitment of an additional 1.5–2.0 million DKK contingency fund (beyond the 10.5 million baseline) explicitly designated for extending phase-two technical work and maintaining coalition engagement through months 18–24 if phase-three institutional gates (published feasibility report, formal engagement with regulators, financing plan) are achieved but AltID procurement influence remains uncertain, allowing the project to sustain momentum without accepting forced wind-down.

Structure phase-three funding as partially conditional on AltID progress and partially unconditional, ensuring that if Danish procurement stalls, at least 2.0 million DKK of the planned 3.5 million phase-three budget is redirected toward EU-level standards work, coalition consolidation, and publication, reducing Danish institutional dependence and creating institutional value regardless of AltID outcome.

Accept the current 10.5 million DKK budget as fixed and establish a clear go/no-go decision gate at month 16, explicitly allowing the project to pivot to lower-cost maintenance mode (coalition engagement, publication, EU-level standards input) if phase-three institutional criteria are not met, treating this pivot not as failure but as strategic redirection toward longer-term leverage and accepting that near-term AltID influence may be unachievable given institutional capture risk.
levers.review_lever: Contingency funding enables resilience but requires securing additional financing before phase two starts, delaying project launch; partial conditionality balances Danish and EU strategic bets but may signal to Danish gatekeepers that the project is hedging its bets; explicit go/no-go pivot avoids sunk-cost escalation but requires stakeholder acceptance of a narrowed near-term scope. None addresses the underlying problem: that project timelines are set by external institutional decisions that the project team cannot directly control.

levers.name: Team Expertise Concentration and Security-Risk Mitigation
levers.consequences: The project's technical credibility and security rigor depend on recruiting researchers with specific expertise in mobile authentication, FIDO2, eIDAS implementation, and adversarial cryptographic design. The budget includes staffing for a lead mobile-security researcher, a regulatory specialist, a policy coordinator, a technical demonstrator lead, and engineering support. However, if the project becomes dependent on one or two individuals who possess irreplaceable expertise (e.g., only one staff member understands GrapheneOS and FIDO2 threat modeling), project resilience collapses if that person leaves, becomes unavailable due to illness, or is blocked by external actors from participating. Conversely, duplicating expertise and spreading knowledge across multiple team members increases overhead costs and complexity but reduces the project's vulnerability to loss of key personnel and improves institutional longevity.
options: Build the team around a single lead mobile-security researcher with recognized expertise and publication record, supported by junior engineers and a policy coordinator, accepting higher person-dependence risk in exchange for faster decision-making, clearer accountability, and lower overhead; establish contingency documentation and knowledge-transfer protocols to mitigate personnel loss risk and plan for coordinated handoff if the lead researcher becomes unavailable.

Recruit pairs of researchers for critical functions (e.g., two senior engineers on mobile authentication and fallback mechanisms, two regulatory specialists on eIDAS and NSIS), deliberately creating redundancy and cross-training so that expertise is distributed and the project can sustain progress if one person departs or is blocked from participation, accepting higher salary costs and coordination overhead in exchange for institutional resilience.

Partner with external contractors and consulting firms (security audit firms, eIDAS implementation consultants) on a task-specific basis rather than hiring senior permanent staff, reducing long-term payroll risk and allowing the project to access specialized expertise on demand, but accepting loss of organizational knowledge between project phases and reduced continuity of technical judgment across the 24-month timeline.
levers.review_lever: Single-expert model maximizes speed and cost efficiency but creates a critical single point of failure if that expert departs; dual-expertise reduces risk but increases salary and coordination burden and may introduce conflicting viewpoints that slow decision-making; external contracting preserves flexibility but prevents deep institutional knowledge accumulation and makes it harder to maintain security standards across demonstrator development. None eliminates the core tension: that building institutional capacity and reducing consultant dependence requires months of ramp-up time that phase one's compressed 8-month timeline may not allow.

levers.name: Publication and Transparency Cadence Versus Institutional Negotiation Discretion
levers.consequences: The project's credibility and external leverage depend on publishing feasibility reports, security audit results, and demonstrator code or architecture documentation; transparency also builds pressure on institutional gatekeepers by allowing public scrutiny and media engagement. However, publishing detailed technical architecture, threat models, or documented institutional resistance before negotiations are complete can give incumbent operators advance warning of arguments they will face and time to organize defensive responses. Early publication also risks exposing the project to premature criticism from competitors or incumbent platform operators, who may use partial or distorted versions of the project's findings to discredit the work before the full institutional case is made. Conversely, deferring publication until phase three risks that institutional decisions are made without public input, reducing democratic accountability and losing the opportunity to shape public discourse around digital identity risks.
options: Adopt a full-transparency model: publish feasibility reports, audit findings, demonstrator code, and policy proposals on a rolling basis as they are completed, making project materials immediately available to civil-society organizations, media, and interested institutions; accept that this approach may trigger early defensive responses from incumbent operators but maximizes public awareness, enables external researchers to validate findings independently, and reduces the project's ability to be surprised or stonewalled by institutional actors.

Sequence publications strategically: defer technical architecture and threat-modeling details until phase two demonstrators are complete and external security audit is finished, publish the feasibility report and policy proposal in month 8 as committed deliverables, and embargo detailed audit findings until after formal engagement with AltID and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen in months 14–16, allowing institutional negotiations to proceed without providing competing arguments advance notice.

Publish aggregate findings and policy recommendations broadly, but keep detailed technical demonstrator code and security analysis restricted to cleared institutional partners (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, AltID teams, security committees) until after phase three decisions are made, treating demonstrators as tools for institutional persuasion rather than as public-domain artifacts, and making the broader case for platform-neutral authentication in policy and academic channels without exposing technical details to incumbent operator scrutiny.
levers.review_lever: Full transparency maximizes democratic accountability and external validation but surrenders tactical negotiation advantage; strategic sequencing balances transparency and institutional leverage but requires disciplined messaging and risks appearing to hide critical findings if the embargo is perceived as excessive; restricted technical access preserves negotiation advantage but undermines the project's credibility as an independent research effort and may be perceived as secretive or undemocratic. All three leave unresolved the question of whether institutional actors will change behavior based on publication alone or whether demonstrable institutional consequences (e.g., media backlash, regulatory investigation) must accompany publication to drive actual change.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Standards Choice
levers.consequences: Selecting between a single integrated platform-neutral demonstrator versus separate mobile and fallback demonstrators determines both technical credibility and resource allocation across phases two and three. A unified demonstrator runs the risk of feature creep and misses the opportunity to isolate fallback mechanisms from mobile OS constraints; separate demonstrators create more friction points but allow stronger evidence that platform-neutral access does not require abandoning mobile security entirely. This choice also signals to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen whether the project is proposing a shadow MitID replacement or a true architectural alternative.
options: Develop a single comprehensive demonstrator using FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS that mimics live MitID workflows, integrating both primary authentication and a built-in fallback path to establish that a unified stack can operate independently of Apple and Google.

Build two decoupled demonstrators: one mobile-focused on GrapheneOS using OpenID Connect and FIDO2 for day-to-day authentication, and a separate browser-based or hardware-token fallback that operates entirely outside the mobile ecosystem, each proving a distinct non-incumbent pathway.

Construct a minimal reference implementation demonstrator that authenticates against a simulated Danish identity provider using open standards, deliberately avoiding feature parity with MitID in order to focus evaluation strictly on platform neutrality and fallback feasibility without inviting scope expansion.
levers.review: Separate demonstrators prove architectural independence but diffuse impact if neither reaches the maturity needed to influence AltID procurement timelines; a single demonstrator risks feature creep and losing focus on the core fallback message. The options do not address how to communicate demonstrator limitations to stakeholders who will expect production-readiness parallels.

levers.name: Coalition Structure and Civil-Society Lead
levers.consequences: Positioning civil-society organizations or academic researchers as public faces of the platform-neutrality push rather than government bodies removes the appearance of state-directed vendor selection and increases credibility with EU counterparts and regulatory bodies concerned about democratic legitimacy. However, this also transfers agenda-setting power away from the project team and may slow institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen if civil-society co-leads pursue privacy or ideological framings that diverge from the project's resilience-and-procurement emphasis. A weak civil-society coalition risks the appearance of a vendor-driven or academic paper exercise rather than a genuine public-interest intervention.
options: Anchor the coalition with a respected Danish civil-society organization such as a privacy advocate or digital rights group as co-lead, with the project team in a technical-support role, and explicitly structure monthly public reporting to maintain independence optics and EU visibility.

Distribute leadership across three nodes: an academic security researcher heading technical work, a civil-society privacy advocate leading public advocacy, and a procurement or resilience specialist engaging Digitaliseringsstyrelsen directly, to create multiple credibility streams without a single point of failure.

Maintain the project team as the primary institutional actor and recruit civil-society and academic advisors into a formal steering committee with public membership and quarterly meetings, reserving procurement engagement for the project lead to ensure message coherence and continuity.
levers.review: Civil-society co-leadership increases legitimacy but diffuses control and may introduce competing narratives that undermine procurement messaging; team-led models with advisory structures risk appearing state-captured if Digitaliseringsstyrelsen is perceived as controlling the agenda. None of the options address how to manage tensions if civil-society partners want stronger public advocacy than procurement timing allows.

levers.name: Phase-Two Demonstrator Platform and Operating-System Choice
levers.consequences: Selecting GrapheneOS, Lineage OS, or another privacy-respecting Android fork versus attempting iOS compatibility or a web-only approach determines the demonstrator's technical defensibility and political acceptability. GrapheneOS carries stronger privacy credentials and independence from Google Play but is less familiar to Danish public-sector evaluators and carries a perception of niche adoption; a broader Android fork reduces that friction but weakens the platform-independence claim if it still relies on Google APIs. A web-only approach avoids OS lock-in entirely but loses credibility in a mobile-first authentication environment where citizens expect app-based security. The choice shapes both technical scope and stakeholder perception of whether fallback pathways are realistic or fringe.
options: Implement the primary demonstrator on GrapheneOS using only GrapheneOS-native security APIs and open-standards authentication, accepting reduced familiarity among Danish stakeholders in exchange for the strongest technical case that mobile authentication does not require Google or Apple dependencies.

Deploy the demonstrator on LineageOS or another widely available Android fork that supports F-Droid app distribution, reducing barriers to stakeholder comprehension while maintaining the core claim that Android-based authentication can operate without Play Store or Google Play Services dependency.

Build a browser-based progressive web app (PWA) or hybrid web/native demonstrator that minimizes OS-level dependencies altogether and works across both iOS and Android through standard web authentication APIs, prioritizing cross-platform accessibility over the statement that mobile OS independence is required.
levers.review: GrapheneOS maximizes platform-independence credibility but introduces adoption and perception barriers among non-specialist evaluators; web-based approaches broaden accessibility but weaken the argument that mobile-OS duopoly dependence is the core problem. The options do not resolve whether demonstrator credibility is measured by technical purity or by stakeholder adoption signals that could compromise the independence message.

levers.name: Engagement Timing and Institutional Lead Target
levers.consequences: Approaching Digitaliseringsstyrelsen early in phase one versus waiting until demonstrators are complete and phase-two evidence is solid determines whether the project influences AltID procurement direction upstream or arrives as a critique of decisions already locked in. Early engagement risks being seen as premature or proposal-driven without technical backing; late engagement maximizes demonstrator credibility but may miss critical procurement-decision windows. The choice also depends on whether MitID's operator or other incumbent bodies perceive the project as collaborative exploration or as a threat to existing contracts and operator revenue. Misaligned timing can result in either dismissal due to lack of evidence or procedural opposition once institutional commitments harden.
options: Initiate formal engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the AltID program office during phase one using the feasibility report and institutional risk framing as the opening conversation, positioning the project as a resilience partner and inviting early procurement language discussions before AltID design is finalized.

Defer direct institutional engagement until the end of phase two when demonstrators and the full feasibility report are complete, then approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen with concrete technical evidence and a formal procurement-language proposal, trading early influence for higher credibility and reduced risk of early dismissal.

Pursue a two-stage engagement: informal early discussions with sympathetic Digitaliseringsstyrelsen staff during phase one to understand procurement timelines and decision gates, followed by formal proposals and demonstrator evidence at critical phase gates, allowing the project to adapt tactics based on institutional receptiveness without premature commitment.
levers.review: Early engagement can shape procurement language but risks premature dismissal if evidence is incomplete; late engagement ensures credibility but may miss decision windows. The options do not address how to recover or pivot if institutional receptiveness shifts due to political or budgetary changes unrelated to the project's merit.

levers.name: EU Standards and Interoperability Positioning
levers.consequences: Framing the platform-neutrality requirement as a European Digital Identity Wallet interoperability and resilience mandate versus a Danish-specific sovereignty concern determines whether the project seeks EU-level standards alignment or focuses narrowly on Danish procurement. EU-level positioning increases the project's legitimacy and difficulty for vendors to dismiss as parochial; it also aligns with Denmark's 2026–2029 strategy and may create pressure on AltID through EU frameworks rather than direct Danish procurement influence. However, EU-level work is slower, requires coordination with multiple member states, and may be pre-empted by incumbent vendor relationships and EU-level standardization bodies already dominated by commercial platforms. A Danish-focused narrative is faster and more controllable but risks being dismissed as a small-country concern that does not generalize.
options: Center phase three on formal submissions and technical comments to the European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and relevant eIDAS2 standards bodies, positioning platform neutrality and fallback access as EU-wide resilience requirements that will set a floor for all member-state implementations including Denmark.

Pursue parallel Danish and EU engagement: maintain AltID-focused procurement language at the Danish level while contributing to EU standards discussions as supporting evidence, avoiding over-commitment to EU-level processes that may not align with Danish phase timelines.

Prioritize Danish AltID and procurement intervention as the primary lever and treat EU engagement as a secondary dissemination channel for demonstrators and feasibility findings, accepting that EU influence is longer-term and lower-probability than direct Danish institutional impact.
levers.review: EU-level positioning increases legitimacy and spreads advocacy pressure but operates on slower timelines that may not align with AltID procurement gates; Danish-focused approaches are faster but risk being dismissed as parochial. The options do not address how to manage misalignment if EU standards work and Danish procurement proceed on incompatible timelines.

levers.name: External Security Review and Third-Party Credibility
levers.consequences: Commissioning an independent security assessment of demonstrators and feasibility findings from a credible external firm or academic institution versus relying on internal review and peer publication increases stakeholder confidence and reduces the risk that Digitaliseringsstyrelsen dismisses the work as self-interested or technically naive. An external review adds cost and timeline delay, and the choice of reviewer shapes perception—a firm with vendor relationships may be perceived as conflicted, while a pure academic body may lack procurement credibility. The review's findings also create a public record that can be cited for or against the project if institutional politics shift, making the timing and scope of external review a strategic choice with political consequences.
options: Commission a formal independent security audit and feasibility assessment from a respected third-party firm such as a Danish or Nordic security consultancy or academic security lab, with public release of findings and explicit scope covering demonstrators, fallback-mechanism soundness, and platform-independence claims.

Pair internal technical review with peer publication in recognized academic conferences and journals, allowing the academic community to vet the work's technical merit while maintaining faster timelines and lower cost than commercial audit, accepting reduced procurement-level credibility.

Engage a panel of external advisors from academia, cybersecurity, and procurement domains for ongoing review throughout phases two and three, publishing findings incrementally rather than a single comprehensive audit, spreading credibility-building across multiple sources and timelines.
levers.review: Commercial external audit maximizes procurement credibility but adds cost and timeline risk; academic peer review is faster and lower-cost but may lack direct procurement influence. The options do not address how to respond if external findings are negative or identify technical gaps that require scope expansion or delay.

levers.name: Fallback Mechanism Design Philosophy and Fallback Trigger Conditions
levers.consequences: Designing the fallback authentication path as a transparent citizen-selectable option available at initial login versus a system-initiated emergency failover triggered only when primary authentication fails determines both user-experience friction and institutional resistance to the fallback requirement. Transparent choice creates a UX and policy narrative that supports genuine optionality and digital autonomy; it also allows supporters to frame fallback as empowerment rather than a compromise path. However, incumbent operators and platform vendors may resist a design that positions platform-dependent authentication as optional rather than default, fearing reduced platform engagement. A system-triggered failover design is less disruptive to incumbent expectations but weakens the political case for platform neutrality by hiding the fallback mechanism and limiting its visibility as a credible alternative. The fallback-trigger conditions also determine whether the fallback path is truly platform-neutral or merely a temporary workaround for edge cases.
options: Design the fallback mechanism as a citizen-facing option available at initial login, allowing users to authenticate through browser-based OpenID Connect or hardware-token methods without requiring the mobile app, with clear labeling of platform dependencies so citizens understand the security and autonomy trade-offs.

Implement the fallback as a system-initiated automatic failover triggered when the primary mobile authentication path fails or is unavailable, maintaining the platform-dependent primary path as default while ensuring fallback capacity exists, positioning resilience as an invisible contingency rather than a citizen choice.

Structure the fallback authentication path as a complete alternative flow with separate enrollment, credential issuance, and public communication, allowing citizens and institutions to treat fallback and primary paths as equally legitimate entry points, with coordinated messaging that platform neutrality is a design principle rather than an emergency measure.
levers.review: Transparent citizen choice maximizes policy legitimacy but invites institutional resistance and complicates adoption messaging; automatic failover reduces friction with incumbents but weakens the political case that platform neutrality is essential. The options do not address how to manage security perception gaps if citizens or evaluators interpret fallback mechanisms as second-class authentication compared to the primary mobile path.

levers.name: Demonstrator Authenticity and Security Pedigree
levers.consequences: The credibility of platform-neutral fallback authentication rests entirely on whether skeptical regulators and operators believe the demonstrators represent genuinely secure alternatives, not security theater or ideological proof-of-concept. A demonstrator built by academic researchers with published cryptographic credentials and external security review generates institutional weight; one built without formal adversarial review or by unknown contributors becomes ammunition for incumbent operators to dismiss as immature or unvetted. The choice determines whether AltID stakeholders and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen treat the work as a credible technical baseline or as activist posturing.
options: Commission an independent third-party security audit (e.g., by a recognized security firm or university security lab with published eIDAS/NSIS expertise) of both demonstrators before phase two completion, with findings published alongside the project outputs to establish institutional credibility and shift the burden of evidence onto platform-dependent alternatives.

Embed a security researcher with established peer-reviewed publication record on mobile authentication, FIDO2, or eIDAS as a co-lead of the demonstrator work, ensuring that cryptographic design and threat modeling are defensible in academic and regulatory contexts from project inception.

Pursue a lightweight self-assessment and fuzzing protocol covering the demonstrators' authentication logic, publish the methodology and results transparently, and invite the security research community to contribute independent validation through a public code repository and open-call bug-bounty period.
levers.review: Third-party audit provides highest institutional weight but delays phase-two timeline and costs 150k–250k DKK; academia-led design builds credibility incrementally but depends on finding a suitable researcher and may not satisfy procurement-minded regulators who want formal certification pathways. All three leave open the gap of productization: demonstrators need not and should not be production-ready, but regulators will use lack of operational maturity against fallback-capable design, regardless of security pedigree.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Posture and Regulatory Window
levers.consequences: Phase two demonstrators are complete by month 16; AltID procurement and technical specifications are being finalized around months 14–18. This window is narrow and non-recoverable—if the project fails to inject platform-neutrality language or fallback-access requirements into AltID design documents or procurement criteria by month 18, the next identity refresh cycle is likely 5–10 years away. Engagement posture determines whether the project appears as a constructive technical contributor (raising AltID resilience) or an external pressure campaign (triggering defensive stonewalling from incumbent operators and procurement gatekeepers). Misjudging tone or timing converts technical work into political liability.
options: Present demonstrators and feasibility findings to AltID's technical working group and procurement team in month 15 as optional resilience enhancements and fallback pathways, framing platform-neutrality as a continuity insurance policy rather than a criticism of existing MitID, and negotiate for inclusion as a non-mandatory secondary authentication layer or contingency plan in procurement language.

Escalate the platform-dependency issue to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's digital-strategy unit and to Finanstilsynet (the financial regulator) in month 14, positioning the demonstrators as evidence supporting mandatory supplier-diversification and fallback requirements in upcoming procurement rules, and use regulatory pressure as leverage to force AltID procurement teams to justify their platform choices.

Withhold direct engagement with AltID until phase two demonstrates working fallback authentication at a technical conference or academic venue, then use external validation and media attention to create a reputational cost for AltID if it ignores platform-neutral alternatives, forcing a late-cycle procurement amendment or design reconsideration driven by public-sector reputation management.
levers.review: Constructive engagement risks being ignored if procurement teams perceive no downside cost to platform dependence; regulatory escalation invites institutional backlash and may harden opposition; public-shaming via external validation depends on media traction and may backfire if perceived as grandstanding rather than substance. None addresses the core blocker: that MitID operators control AltID's technical direction and have financial incentives to perpetuate platform duopoly lock-in.

levers.name: Fallback-Mechanism Role and Certification Pathway
levers.consequences: A fallback authentication path can be positioned as either a mandatory, always-available alternative to app-based authentication (requiring formal certification and integration into MitID or AltID trust frameworks) or as an optional, contingency-only mechanism (triggered only if primary path fails, reducing certification burden but also reducing institutional weight and pre-emptive impact). The former increases relevance and guarantees that the fallback is actually deployed and maintained; the latter preserves optionality and avoids forcing MitID operators to defend why their primary path is not platform-neutral. The positioning shapes whether the project influences day-to-day authentication behavior or remains a theoretical insurance policy that operators and citizens ignore unless forced to use it.
options: Design the fallback mechanism as a mandatory secondary authentication option available to all citizens for critical transactions (e.g., tax filing, medical data access), require formal integration into MitID's or AltID's certification and trust-evaluation framework, and pursue formal approval from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen as a regulatory requirement rather than an optional feature.

Position the fallback mechanism as a declared contingency path activated only during documented platform outages or supplier policy changes that affect citizen access, reducing immediate certification friction but requiring pre-positioned legal and technical infrastructure so that fallback deployment does not become a multi-month crisis response if the contingency is triggered.

Develop the fallback as a progressive-enhancement fallback embedded in the browser-based eIDAS2 wallet reference architecture rather than as a MitID alternative, allowing it to exist in the EU standards layer and circumvent formal Danish MitID certification gates, accepting lower near-term institutional impact in exchange for longer-term EU-level influence over digital identity portability.
levers.review: Mandatory integration forces a choice that incumbent operators will resist; contingency-only positioning reduces pressure but risks abandonment if the contingency never materializes; EU-layer design avoids Danish gatekeepers but delays measurable impact on AltID and leaves Danish citizens exposed for years. All three leave unresolved the question of whether citizens or regulators will actually use a fallback mechanism if it exists—convenience and habit favor the incumbent duopoly even if alternatives are available.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Advocacy Leadership
levers.consequences: A coalition spanning civil-society privacy advocates, contingency-planning authorities, academic security researchers, and sympathetic MPs creates multiple institutional entry points for platform-neutrality arguments and reduces the project's appearance as a single-organization campaign. The coalition's composition also signals credibility: an organization led by privacy advocates may be dismissed as ideological; one led by contingency-planning authorities or a public-health regulator concerned with medical data access gains operational legitimacy. Conversely, a broad coalition risks diffuse messaging, competing priorities, and paralysis-by-consensus if partners disagree on whether to prioritize resilience, privacy, sovereignty, or cost reduction.
options: Establish a formal steering group co-led by a contingency-planning or crisis-management authority (e.g., Beredskabsstyrelsen or a regional health authority) and an established privacy or civil-rights organization, ensuring that the coalition's public-facing narrative emphasizes continuity-of-service and public-sector resilience rather than ideology, and securing institutional credibility from a government agency with explicit responsibility for backup systems and supply-chain risk.

Build a looser, decentralized coalition of individual researchers, security experts, and interested MPs rather than formal partner organizations, allowing faster decision-making and preventing institutional veto power, but accepting reduced formal institutional weight and a greater burden on the project's communications team to synthesize and coordinate messaging across independent voices.

Prioritize recruitment of technical leads from major Danish banks and critical-infrastructure operators (e.g., energy or transportation authorities) that depend on digital identity authentication for internal compliance and customer access, creating a private-sector counterweight to public-sector incumbent operators and positioning fallback authentication as a business-continuity requirement rather than a regulatory or advocacy issue.
levers.review: Government co-leadership provides credibility but introduces slow decision cycles and political sensitivity; decentralized coalition enables speed but risks public perception of disorganization; private-sector engagement shifts framing but may alienate civil-society partners and create suspicion of commercial motivations. None directly addresses the core institutional asymmetry: that incumbent MitID and AltID operators have formal decision authority while the coalition has only advocacy pressure.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Sovereignty Framing
levers.consequences: The project's policy narrative can emphasize either continuity-of-service and supplier-concentration risk (resonates with procurement and risk-management officials) or digital sovereignty and reduced foreign-vendor lock-in (resonates with privacy advocates and nationalist constituencies but invites dismissal as ideological). A resilience frame centers on "what if Apple or Google change terms, restrict access, or experience regional outages?" and appeals to institutional duty to protect essential services. A sovereignty frame centers on "Danish public infrastructure should not depend on foreign corporate decisions" and appeals to democratic control but risks being labeled as xenophobic or anti-American, playing into incumbent operators' dismissal of the project as a political stunt rather than a serious security proposal.
options: Lead all policy communication and proposal language with continuity-of-service, supplier-concentration, and business-continuity framing—emphasizing that fallback authentication is insurance against platform-policy changes, outages, or geopolitical disruption—and minimize or omit sovereignty language unless specifically asked, allowing resilience arguments to dominate institutional decision-making without appearing ideologically motivated.

Frame platform-dependency as a democratic accountability and public-interest issue, emphasizing that foreign corporations should not control the trust anchors for Danish citizens' access to public services and healthcare, and ground the argument in European digital autonomy principles and eIDAS intent to reduce digital dependence on large U.S. platforms, accepting that this frame will energize privacy and digital-rights communities but may alienate procurement-focused officials.

Explicitly connect both frames in project materials—present resilience and continuity as the primary institutional rationale, but also articulate digital sovereignty as a secondary strategic objective for Denmark's 2026–2029 digital strategy, treating them as complementary rather than competing, and allow different audiences to weight them differently based on institutional mandate and values.
levers.review: Pure resilience framing maximizes institutional buy-in but may be perceived as euphemistic if sovereignty is the actual primary concern; sovereignty framing energizes political allies but invites institutional dismissal as activist rather than technical; dual framing attempts to satisfy both but risks appearing incoherent or opportunistic. None fully resolves the perception problem: that the project is fundamentally a challenge to incumbent operators' market position, regardless of stated rationale.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Input Versus Danish-Focused Procurement Intervention
levers.consequences: The project can allocate effort either toward influencing European Digital Identity Wallet standards, interoperability requirements, and eIDAS2 implementation rules (higher institutional reach, longer timelines, lower direct impact on Danish AltID) or toward directly engaging Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, MitID operators, and AltID procurement (faster feedback loop, higher direct impact, but limited to Danish institutional scope and dependent on political will of a small number of gatekeepers). EU-level work builds on the project's technical credibility and creates pressure on member states to adopt supplier-neutral requirements; Danish-focused work concentrates effort on the immediate decision window but accepts that a negative outcome at the Danish level cannot be overridden by EU standards later.
options: Prioritize direct engagement with Danish procurement, AltID technical teams, and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen through months 14–20, treating EU standards input as a secondary activity that leverages successful Danish precedent; accept that if Danish institutional capture occurs, the project's EU-level work becomes a consolation prize rather than the primary lever for system change.

Allocate 40–50% of phase-three effort toward formal input to the European Digital Identity Wallet technical working group, eIDAS2 national-implementation committees, and relevant EU standardization bodies (ETSI, CEN), positioning platform-neutral and fallback-capable requirements as EU-level best practices and accepting slower but broader impact that may influence Danish procurement indirectly through regulatory harmonization pressure.

Treat EU engagement and Danish procurement as parallel tracks with equal resourcing, ensuring that the project is simultaneously pressuring Danish gatekeepers and building EU-level language that makes it harder for Denmark to ignore platform-neutrality requirements, accepting overhead complexity and the risk that neither track reaches critical mass if team capacity proves insufficient to maintain momentum on both fronts.
levers.review: EU-first strategy accepts weak near-term Danish impact in exchange for longer-term systemic change; Danish-first strategy risks wasting EU relationship-building effort if Danish procurement is captured; parallel tracks optimize total leverage but demand senior staff capable of navigating both Danish institutional politics and EU technical governance, a skillset gap that may not be filled within the project budget.

levers.name: Fallback Technical Architecture and Platform Dependency Trade-off
levers.consequences: A browser-based fallback authentication mechanism avoids mobile-OS dependence entirely but introduces new dependencies on web-browser vendors (Chrome, Safari) and may exclude citizens without reliable broadband or digital literacy for web authentication workflows. A hardware-token or smartcard-based fallback avoids both mobile and browser dependencies but requires physical distribution, enrollment overhead, and citizen willingness to carry an additional device—a friction cost that may limit actual adoption. A GrapheneOS-based mobile demonstrator proves that a privacy-respecting Android alternative is technically feasible but doesn't eliminate mobile-OS dependence and may face institutional resistance because GrapheneOS is perceived as niche or security-theater rather than a sustainable citizen-facing solution. The choice determines whether the fallback is truly platform-neutral or merely swaps one dependency set for another.
options: Develop the browser-based fallback mechanism as the primary technical pathway, emphasizing that web-based authentication using OpenID Connect and FIDO2 over HTTPS is the closest available path to platform-neutrality for mass-market citizen authentication, and position the GrapheneOS demonstrator as a proof-of-concept showing that mobile alternatives exist but acknowledging that browser-based workflows are more institutionally feasible.

Implement a hybrid fallback combining a lightweight hardware token (USB-C or NFC-based, compatible with existing national ID cards if technically feasible) with web-browser authentication, creating multiple independent fallback pathways so that citizens can choose based on preference and circumstance, and accepting additional complexity in demonstrator scope and certification requirements in exchange for true platform-neutrality across device types.

Prioritize the GrapheneOS-based mobile fallback as the lead technical pathway, arguing that a privacy-respecting, open-source Android variant demonstrates that app-based authentication need not depend on Google's proprietary systems and integrity APIs, and position the browser-based approach as a secondary fallback, accepting that this choice keeps fallback authentication within the mobile-OS ecosystem but substitutes open-source infrastructure for proprietary platform control.
levers.review: Browser-based avoids OS lock-in but introduces new browser-vendor dependencies and digital-divide friction; hardware tokens offer true platform-independence but have high adoption friction and cost; GrapheneOS remains OS-dependent despite being open-source and may not satisfy regulatory demands for mainstream platform alternatives.
